act.statement: Allow pharmacists to treat more sicknesses and conditions

summary.why: This party says that pharmacists have capacity that GPs and other health services may not. Increasing the number of conditions that pharmacists can prescribe or provide care for without needing approval from a doctor or nurse will make it easier for people managing long-term conditions or those with straightforward sicknesses with clear diagnosis. This would reduce wait times for GPs and provide quicker care.
summary.how: This party would list more sicknesses and ailments pharmacists are allowed to treat, including sore throats, tonsillitis, gout and period pain. There would be a protocol for when pharmacists should refer back to a doctor for treatment. Consultation fees would remain capped at $20 for most and $5 for Community Service Card holders.

sources.title: 'Your pharmacist should be your first stop', 6 August 2026 (accessed 06 August 2026)

act.statement: Remove some rules around pharmacy locations, ownership and licences

summary.why: This party says that removing the rule that prevents a single person or entity from owning more than five pharmacies would make it easier to open new pharmacies. Changing other rules about pharmacy locations, licenses and qualifications for pharmacists would make it easier to open and staff pharmacies anywhere in the country.
summary.how: The party would change regulatory settings to implement the reforms. Online prescription e-lockers can be used to help those in rural areas access medication when pharmacies may have limited opening hours.

sources.title: 'Your pharmacist should be your first stop', 6 August 2026 (accessed 06 August 2026)

act.statement: Require a minimum three-year sentence for anyone convicted of burglary three times

summary.why: This party says that most people who are released from prison for burglary end up in prison again within two years. By making longer sentences without parole mandatory, burglary will be prevented and people with convictions for burglary will reoffend less.
summary.how: This party would make receiving a third conviction of burglary or a single conviction for three counts of burglary would require a minimum sentence of three years in prison, with no home detention, parole or early release. Judges would use discretion for the length of sentence, between three and ten years. An aggravated burglary would count both for three strikes for violent crime and three strikes for burglary.

act.statement: Increase the percentage of the health budget spent on Pharmac to over 10 percent by 2033

summary.why: This party says that many medications for conditions like cancer are publicly funded in Australia but not in NZ. The public drug funding system Pharmac, is not receiving enough funding to keep up. Paying for medication can reduce pressure elsewhere in the health system by helping people manage their health conditions effectively.
summary.how: This party would increase funding for Pharmac by 1 percent per year until 2033, from the current base of 4.9 percent of the health budget. More medications on Pharmac's "options for investment" list would become available to New Zealanders. A sustainable funding option would mean Pharmac can spend money on drugs for more health conditions.  This party estimates that this policy would cost over $4bn over 7 years.

act.statement: Increase the areas of conservation land which can be accessed by helicopter for hunting

summary.why: This party says that in areas of forest and mountains where people want to hunt, there are "no-fly" and "no-landing" areas for helicopters with no clear reasoning. In areas where helicopters are the fastest way in, access restrictions should be justified with obvious safety or conservation reasons.
summary.how: This party would allow the Game Council to designate helicopter landing sites, and restrict commercial venison operators by animal gender when necessary, leaving trophy stags for hunters. DOC would be required to use public tests to designate where aircraft could land, and would not have any say in which types of helicopters were used. The Outdoors Access Commission would be asked to make hunting access a priority in its work programme.

act.statement: Prevent universities from allocating support of any kind based on ethnicity

summary.why: This party says that previous policy directions have required that public agencies should allocate services based on individual need and value, rather than race. Universities should be included in this directive too, as universities are independent but largely funded by the taxpayer. Grants or donations from private money would be exempt from this requirement.
summary.how: This party would amend the Education and Training Act, adding language preventing benefits or support being offered on the basis of race of ethnicity. This would include scholarships, accommodation support, designated spaces in tertiary institutions and any other types of support. Universities would still be able to confer scholarships based on academic merit, need, geographic location, economic circumstances or disability.

act.statement: Make the abuse of a companion animal in a family violence situation a crime

summary.why: This party says that pets are being threatened and abused to coerce people in family violence situations and prevent them from leaving. Research shows half of victims delay leaving a violent situation because they are concerned about their pets. Criminalising the abuse of animals in this context will give Police more tools to protect victims. States in Australia and the US have enacted similar laws and New Zealand needs to do the same.
summary.how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to make abusing a pet with the goal of coercion an offence punishable by a maximum seven years in prison. Protection orders would be strengthened to ensure offenders cannot control access to a pet and ensure pets are not left with abusers. Police would be required to record the presence of pets in a family violence situation and receive clear operational guidance around removing pets to a safe place if the animal is at risk of harm.

sources.title: 'Stop Coercion by Animal Abuse', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

act.statement: Ensure agriculture is not part of the emissions trading scheme

summary.why: This party says that New Zealand's dairy industry has a lower emissions footprint than the global average. Adding methane emissions from dairy farming to the Emissions Trading Scheme would make producing dairy more expensive and mean more dairy production happens in other countries. New Zealand should be increasing dairy production instead of reducing it to limit emissions. The Paris Agreement is not fit for purpose.
summary.how: This party would continue to exclude emissions from the agriculture sector from the Emissions Trading Scheme. Agriculture would be permanently excluded. This policy would be part of a changed approach to New Zealand's commitments under the Paris Agreement.

act.statement: Count carbon dioxide and methane differently under emissions targets

summary.why: This party says that carbon dioxide and methane both contribute to global heating. Carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere longer than methane, which is largely produced by the dairy and sheep industries.
summary.how: This party would rewrite NZ's Nationally Determined Contributions plan, which is required by the Paris Agreement. It would differentiate between the emissions caused by methane and carbon dioxide so that methane emissions do not have to be reduced by the same degree as carbon emissions. A "split gas approach" would calculate the emissions generated by carbon dioxide and methane differently. Carbon dioxide emissions would be reduced while methane levels could continue at current levels.

act.statement: Make disrupting lawful hunters with drones or by standing in the line of fire an offence

summary.why: This party says that people can disrupt hunters by stepping into the line of fire, or disturbing game birds with a drone. This should not happen if a hunter is following legal guidelines and safety protocols. While people are free to protest hunting, those protests should not place anyone at risk.  It says that currently there are no laws covering this situation which needs to change.
summary.how: This party would create specific infringement offences for standing in the line of fire of a hunter, and for disturbing game birds with aircraft like drones or helicopters. These infringements would not apply if the hunter was not following the relevant laws and guidelines.

act.statement: Issue licences for security professionals to have more authority against intrusion or theft

summary.why: This party says that there are twice as many security guards as police officers in New Zealand, but security guards don't have any legal authority. People who do not feel safe in shops buy online instead, impacting small businesses. Licencing trained and vetted security guards to remove people and use proportionate force when necessary would be good for businesses worried about crime. It would accompany current law reforms allowing people to make citizens arrests if no police are present.
summary.how: This party would train vetted security guards; those who complete the training would be issued with a special licence. The licence would allow them to require a person's name an address to enter a premise; issue up to 3-year exclusion notices for a premise or premises; remove people who are threatening or breaching entry conditions; carry out safety searches individuals would have to consent to as a condition of entry; if necessary, use force, until the person complies or the police arrive. Licenced security professionals would have the ability to detain someone while waiting for the police.

act.statement: Give the Game Council responsibility for game animals on conservation land

summary.why: This party says that legislation currently treats deer as pest animals to be exterminated rather than game animals to be hunted. The Game Council can advise DOC but does not make decisions. Hunters spend time in the area where these animals live and should be making decisions about what happens to game animals on conservation land.
summary.how: This party would transfer responsibility for game animals from DOC to the Game Council. It would also give the Council more funding to recognise its further responsibilities.

act.statement: Recognise introduced game species in law

summary.why: This party says that game animals on NZ's conservation land are treated as pests which should be killed. However, these animals are valuable to many rural communities and hunters and should be treated as natural resources instead. Hunters can strike a balance between removing game animals to protect the natural environment and ensuring there are enough game for the future.
summary.how: This party would change legislation to designate game animals and birds as natural resources rather than pests. Herds of New Zealand deer, which hunters appreciate, would be designated as specific "Herds of Special Interest" for protection. The whitetail deer on Stewart Island would be given this designation.

act.statement: Limit the number of branded items in school uniforms to reduce costs

summary.why: This party says that in 2025, 38,000 WINZ hardship loans were issued to help families cover the cost of school uniforms, and in some cases the combined cost for school uniforms is over $1,000. Limiting state schools to just three branded school items will make uniforms more affordable for New Zealanders. Generic items such as socks would be available from low-cost retailers like The Warehouse or KMart. School uniforms can promote school culture but expensive uniforms don't improve educational outcomes, and similar policies in parts of Australia and the UK have been successful.
summary.how: This party would limit state schools to three mandatory branded items as part of a uniform. Alternative, generic options for clothes like skirts, shirts, trousers and socks could be selected from low-cost retail stores. This policy would only apply to everyday items worn to school, not to more special items like branded clothing for sports teams.

act.statement: Allow children to take any passing school bus, not just buses specifically for one school

summary.why: This party says that school transport rules are based on the nearest school. Parents who choose different schools for reasons like siblings being close together may not be able to use a school bus service. This is particularly difficult for families in rural areas. Allowing children to ride any school bus with space would make it easier for families.
summary.how: This party would introduce a rule where a child living along an existing school bus route could use any available seat. If a bus route became full, another one would be provided by the Ministry of Education. Any extra funding would come from the education budget by cutting other spending.

sources.title: 'Let the Kid on the Bus ', undated

act.statement: Give volunteer groups more opportunities and funding for maintenance on conservation land

summary.why: This party says that that DOC has a 30 percent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021. Volunteer groups carry out track and hut maintenance, but should receive funding for this over multiple years rather than applying annually. Creating a system for groups to receive biodiversity credits will incentivise further volunteer work in the hills.
summary.how: This party would require DOC to give community groups the first opportunity for funding for maintenance on conservation land. Community groups would be allowed to sign multi-year contracts for work they are able to do. If biodiversity benefits were independently verified, groups including hunters would receive biodiversity credits. The Game Council and Deerstalkers Association would be formally represented when deciding how animals on conservation land were managed.

act.statement: Return $1 to local authorities for each night an international tourist spends in their area

summary.why: This party says that millions of tourists come to New Zealand, but these visitors can place pressure on local infrastructure. International visitors pay a levy that is collected by central government, but local government needs funding for infrustructure costs like roads and wastewater. Any new taxes or expenses should be very specifically targeted to where they are needed without making things more expensive for residents and ratepayers.
summary.how: This party would use a data programme to determine where international visitors are staying. Each year, the central government would make an automatic annual payment of $1 for each night an international visitor spent in that council area. This dividend could replace some increases to rates which would otherwise pay for infrastructure upgrades. Based on 2026 nights, this would include $8.2m for Auckland, $4.9m for Queenstown and $2m for Rotorua.

sources.title: 'ACT is supporting local tourism, not new taxes ', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'ACT sets the No New Taxes agenda', 8 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

act.statement: Create a regulatory framework for the use of cryptocurrency

summary.why: This party says that it's important to support innovation in the NZ financial system. The party claims that cryptocurrency help businesses engage in the global market. The party argues that the government should regulate digital financial assets to facilitate smoother capital investment while ensuring consumer protection and legality. It wants to ensure legitimate businesses have access to banking and are not turned away due to the novel use of cryptocurrency.
summary.how:
This party would establish clear legal and tax rules for cryptocurrency. Such regulation would define what regulated digital currency is. It would review NZ financial regulations to gauge whether current settings deny legitimate businesses access to banking. The party seeks to scale regulation by firm size. 

The party would allow smaller firms a license to experiment with cryptocurrency. This license would exist under government supervision.

sources.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Digital Economy' (PDF), 27 August 2026 (accessed 28 August 2026)

act.statement: Create tax exemptions for use of cryptocurrency

summary.why: This party says that incentivise and provide stability for those seeking to invest in cryptocurrency for the long term.  The party says it wants to simplify and minimise tax compliance complications for everyday users.
summary.how: This party would introduce exemptions for low-value purchases made using cryptocurrency. This party would apply exemptions for the first twelve months of investments that qualify as personal investments in cryptocurrency. Business investments would remain fully taxable.

sources.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Digital Economy' (PDF), 27 August 2026 (accessed 28 August 2026)

act.statement: Add a physical presence test to permanent residents

summary.why: This party says that people need to be regularly living in NZ to be regarded as a permanent resident. They need to show an ongoing connection to NZ.
summary.how: This party would remove the permanent resident visa category and instead change the resident visa to mandate residents to live 2 out of 5 years in NZ. Exemptions will exist for service members, employees of NZ-owned businesses, and certain family commitments.

sources.title: 'ACT’s New Immigration Policy To Put ‘Reside’ Back In ‘Resident’', 1 September 2026 (accessed 01 September 2026)

act.statement: Make Student Service Fees voluntary

summary.why: This party says that voluntary student membership of student associations at universities has been undermined by compulsory 'service fees.' The party says these fees add costs for students that should be paid as they use the services. Instead, the party argues that service fees force students to fund union campaigns and media services that not all students support.
summary.how: This party would change regulations so that services are offered as a menu. Students would then select what services they wish to use. This would prohibit compulsory service fees used to fund services traditionally funded by student unions/associations.

sources.title: 'ACT to campaign on making Student Services Fees voluntary', 10 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Scale back the use and effect of Treaty principles in legislation

summary.why: This party says that, to protect democratic majority rule, judges cannot be allowed to enable Treaty principles to go beyond what Parliament intended. Greater clarity in legislation and removing Treaty considerations would provide greater protection of individual property rights and prevent ethnicity-based equity measures.
summary.how:
This party would add three principles to the Constitution Act. These would be that Parliament is the highest legal authority in NZ; the rule of law is fundamental; and all New Zealanders are equal before the law.  It would also insert property rights into the New Zealand Bill of Rights to ensure homes, farms, businesses and other property are protected.
Tikanga could be used in court only when it was relevant to a case, or where Parliament has expressly provided for it.

sources.title: 'One Law for All, One Future Together', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal' (PDF), 10 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)
'One Law for All Policy' (PDF), 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)
One Law for All. One Future Together.

act.statement: Remove ethnicity-based criteria for delivering public services

summary.why: The party says the only criterion for a person receiving publicly funded services should be need, rather than equity across different groups.
summary.how: The party would create a clear statutory duty that public services are delivered based on need, without group-based equity considerations changing the Public Service Act. Agencies would be required to comply with the principle as a matter of law, and decisions that breach it could be subject to judicial review.

sources.title: 'One Public Service for All ' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Remove group-based equity measures from recruitment in the public sector

summary.why: This party says that that group-based equity measures, such as hiring people of specific ethnic backgrounds, are unneeded. Group-based considerations cannot exist alongside merit-based recruitment.
summary.how: This party would repeal group-based requirements on government departments as employers. It would repeal Section 73 of the Public Service Act, and its equivalent in the Crown Entities Act.

sources.title: 'One Public Service for All ' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Prevent cultural practices from being used in the public service

summary.why: This party says that taxpayers' time and money should not be spent on cultural practices that some staff may not want to do, like prayers and karakia. The party says that cultural skills should only matter as part of a job if absolutely necessary and should not distract from the primary responsibility employees have. Employees should express cultural or spiritual practices like prayers or karakia outside of the workplace.
summary.how: This party would prohibit cultural or spiritual practices in the workplace of public institutions. It would use a clear letter of expectations to the Public Service Commissioner and Cabinet to enforce the removal of cultural expectations.

sources.title: 'One Public Service for All ' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Reduce number of ministries into consolidated departments

summary.why: This party says that countries with a similar population to NZ have fewer government ministries.Merging existing ministries can reduce duplication of responsibility. It says that government spending increases are associated with the number of ministers in a government.
summary.how: This party would to reduce the number of ministries by over half with one senior minister responsible for more areas. Other minister positions that are cut will become junior minister roles below the senior minister.

sources.title: 'ACT unveils plan for radically simpler smaller government ', 28 June 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
ACT’s plan for a consolidated bureaucracy

act.statement: Restrict how many people recieve medical certification for health-related benefits

summary.why: This party says that many people need to get away from sickness benefits and into work. It claims that the country doesn't want to miss out on their potential.
summary.how: This party would make all health and disability benefits subject to approval from an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors. The party would have assessments be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion. Reassessment would begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic. Other reassessments would be phased in with the new criteria for existing Jobseeker Support, health conditions or disabilities and Supported Living Payment.

sources.title: 'ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life', 28 June 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
Welfare as a Hand Up, not a Way of Life

act.statement: Monitor spending for jobseekers receiving a benefit for more than 4 months

summary.why: This party says that there is a need for greater fairness in the welfare system. Some beneficiaries spend money in ways that do not prepare them for work, such as gambling, alcohol and tobacco. The party argues that taxpayers should not fund the purchasing of products that set people back from potentially finding employment.
summary.how: This party would require that people on a jobseeker benefit for 4 months be automatically shifted onto an electronic money management card system. Such a system would block expenses related to smoking, drinking, and gambling. Carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.

sources.title: 'ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life', 28 June 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
Welfare as a Hand Up, not a Way of Life

act.statement: Create a "Working with Children" card

summary.why: This party says it can take up to 3 years for complaints about worker conduct to reach an employer. The party claims that current checks only capture a snapshot in time and not ongoing accountability.
summary.how: This party would create a Working with Children card. Eligibility for the card would take into account relevant criminal convictions, disciplinary findings and other records relating to children or child-related work. If a cardholder is charged with a disqualifying offence, their card could be suspended or revoked, and their employer notified. This would simplify the system for employers and ensure child safety mechanisms can react in real time.

sources.title: 'ACT will introduce smarter screening to improve child safety ', 17 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Establish a public-private partnership to build two independent cancer centres.

summary.why: This party says that cancer is an issue that affects so many families. Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year; by 2044, that number is expected to exceed 45,000.
summary.how: This party would build two centres, built in Christchurch and Auckland. These would be financed through public-private partnerships, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment and other private capital. The investment would be accompanied by a government-run independent philanthropic foundation to help secure additional investment.  This party estimates that this policy would cost 2 billion in baseline capital expenditure.

sources.title: 'ACT unveils plan for New Zealand’s first dedicated Cancer centre - Beyond Tomorrow', 21 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)
Beyond Tomorrow – A Starship for Cancer

act.statement: Prevent any banning of VPNs

summary.why: This party says that claims that VPNs are a key means of privacy protection for journalists, commercial, and personal information. The technology is part of modern cyber-security and should be accessible to the public.
summary.how: This party would not allow VPN bans to be part of any coalition agreement. The party claims it would oppose any VPN ban included in legislation banning children from social media.

sources.title: 'Act will stop any VPN ban', 7 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Allow "innovation trials" for new technology not covered by NZ law

summary.why: This party says that NZ is falling behind because innovative technology like driverless cars and drones available overseas remains illegal. It argues that NZ policy settings are not responsive to change and need greater flexibility. Results from these trials could to help bolster the evidence base for regulatory change.
summary.how: This party would create an application process that would see a singular business be exempt from a particular regulation. The approval would state the safety conditions and how the result will be measured. The Ministry for Regulation would help to run the trials, and companies working in the fields of novel medical technology, drones for agricultural use or driverless cars would be invited to test out this technology.

act.statement: Establish a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas

summary.why: This party says that those on temporary work visas use infrastructure and should help fund its investment. The party claims its tax would raise $80m annually; the NZ temporary work visa would remain cheaper than in both the UK and Australia.
summary.how: This party would add the tax on top of existing taxes. Such a process would be automated through the link between visas and employers.

sources.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand

act.statement: Deport serious offenders who are not New Zealand citizens

summary.why: This party says it wishes to remove dangerous people from society. In addition, it aims to build greater trust in both law and order and immigration.
summary.how: This party would deport Resident Visa holders convicted of offences carrying sentences of 10 years or more, irrespective of how long they have lived in the country. The party specifies that naturalised citizens would not be deported.

sources.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand

act.statement: Introduce benefits stand-down for first years of residence visa

summary.why: This party says that that it is unfair for New Zealanders to fund benefits for people who've only recently committed to living and working in NZ. The party claims its change will prevent any encouragement of welfare dependency among new arrivals.
summary.how: The party would have residence-class visa holders made ineligible for all welfare benefits for the first five years. The party claims it would do so by changing the eligibility criteria that presently permit residence-class visa holders to access welfare benefits.

sources.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand

act.statement: Give teachers legal powers to remove disruptive students from class

summary.why: This party says that disruptive students can be a risk to the safety of other students and teaching staff, distracting others from learning during valuable teaching time.
summary.how: This party would amend legislation so that teachers have an explicit legal power to direct a seriously or persistently disruptive student to leave and go to a staffed, supervised space. A refusal would be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refused again after escalation, staff would be able to use reasonable force to remove them. The current Act would be clarified to allow reasonable and proportionate intervention to prevent harm or the destruction of property. Parents could be fined and authorities involved if they do not attend meetings with their child.

sources.title: 'Disrupt the Class, Leave the Class', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)
Strengthening teacher authority and stopping class disruption

act.statement: Apply English language requirements for accredited employer work visas

summary.why: This party says that migrants who come to NZ should have a solid base-level understanding of the country's most-used language. By ensuring greater English language proficiency, the party promises to increase public trust in the immigration system.
summary.how: This party would extend existing English language requirements to all Accredited Employer Work Visa candidates. It would  exempt seasonal workers.

sources.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand

act.statement: Cut commitments, legislation and measures that lower emissions

summary.why: This party says that emission reduction targets and the emissions trading scheme (ETS) are too costly for New Zealanders. The party cites that trading partners and competitors are not making the same commitments. Additionally, the party cites failed auctions for carbon credits due to purchasing carbon being too expensive under the ETS.
summary.how: This party would repeal the Zero Carbon Act that commits NZ to net zero by 2050. Instead, the party claims that it would tie the emissions cap to the average of NZ's major trading partners. The party would also cut the government's price floor in the ETS. This would lower the costs of carbon emissions for polluting firms.

'Only ACT will cut the Carbon Tax', 8 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)
Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax

act.statement: Increase support for businesses and households affected by the emissions trading scheme

summary.why: This party says that revenue from the emissions trading scheme is just another means by which the government raises revenue, and damages business competitiveness. The party seeks instead to refund the revenue generated to New Zealanders. The party additionally seeks to support businesses most affected by competitiveness concerns. The party is also concerned with the construction of carbon forests as an inefficient use of land.
summary.how: The party would refund revenue derived from ETS auctions to citizens. Industrial carbon assistance would be raised to 90 percent and 60 percent rates where businesses face carbon-cost disadvantages.  The party would remove mandates for carbon forests, with the intention to use that land for farming instead.

act.statement: Add annual expiry dates to accredited employer visas

summary.why: This party says that some businesses depend on migrant workers, creating a barrier to employment for New Zealanders. Adding an automatic expiry to accredited employer visas and requiring evidence of sustained need from the employer would ensure businesses hire New Zealanders when possible.
summary.how: This party would add a 12-month expiration date to the accredited employer visa. For a migrant worker to remain eligible, the employer would need to provide up-to-date evidence of demand.

sources.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand

act.statement: Make Uber and DoorDash-like platform companies provide evidence of work rights

summary.why: This party says that there are as many as 20,980 known overstayers in NZ. Platform apps like Uber and DoorDash do not require evidence of work rights for their drivers, which are needed irrespective of employment status. It is concerned that platform apps can encourage illegal overstaying.
summary.how: This party would establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand. Platform employers such as Uber and DoorDash would be required to verify and report work rights. Employers who facilitate overstaying would lose accreditation.

sources.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand

act.statement: Expand rural policing

summary.why: This party says that there is a lack of reporting of rural crime in NZ. It attributes this to a lack of trust in whether police will investigate. The prosecution rate is presently at 15%.  The lack of enforcement encourages rural crime.
summary.how: This party would provide additional funding to expand the 111 service and hire more officers for rural areas, with a target of an additional 100,000 extra patrol hours each year. It would establish a dedicated rural crime unit.

act.statement: Prevent professionals from being disciplined for expressing opinions outside of their practice

summary.why: This party says that treaty and cultural standards as both unnecessary and an improper rationale for disciplinary action. The party is concerned that standards can encroach deeply personal individual views on contentious political matters.
summary.how: This party would ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice. It says this would protect free speech and expression. It would require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues. Mandatory training would be restricted to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety, and there would be judicial oversight so courts could rein in regulators that went beyond their legal powers.

sources.title: 'Free Speech for Regulated Professionals', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

act.statement: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are resolved

summary.why: This party says that following the completion of the treaty settlement process, reparations for treaty violations by the Crown would be complete. It describes the ongoing influence of the Waitangi Tribunal on current government decisions as overreach by the courts over democratically elected political leaders.
summary.how: This party would amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so that the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed. Once all settlements and claims lodged by the existing statutory deadline of 1 September 2008 are completed, the Waitangi Tribunal should be disestablished. The party argues that redress should be final so the country can move forward, leaving past grievances behind.

sources.title: 'Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal', 10 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

act.statement: Focus National Land Transport Fund on road infrastructure only

summary.why: This party says infrastructure should have its funding protected so that governments cannot redirect its revenue for other purposes. People have paid the fuel tax expecting it to fund the road infrastructure they use, as opposed to other priorities. Mana Whenua considerations, non-functional art, monuments, and decorative amenities on roads should also be excluded for this same reason.
summary.how: This party would legislate that the National Land Transport Fund be used only for road-related infrastructure. The party would also amend procurement rules to not favour any group over another.

act.statement: Require infrastructure projects to consider a cheaper option

summary.why: This party says that potential infrastructure projects, when seeking approval, should be required to publish a lowest-cost safe option alongside the preferred option. Both options should include cost, delivery time, and benefit-cost ratio for each. The party says this is to assess whether the preferred design is taking unnecessary steps or being made with overly conservative assumptions.
summary.how: This party would mandate affordability and efficacy standards, made through the comparison with a cheaper alternative design, be applied to all infrastructure projects seeking government approval.

act.statement: Require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans

summary.why: This party says that councils are responsible for housing developments, while central government is responsible for state highways. Because of these different priorities, housing projects can occur without central government having to build the road capacity to deal with the increased growth. This worsens traffic, travel times and bus networks.
summary.how: This party would require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans. These plans would guarantee funding mechanisms such as road charges, tolls, developer contributions, council funding and private capital to ensure road capacity keeps up with population growth.

act.statement: Introduce an affordability test on used-car import regulations

summary.why: This party says that regulations for used cars being imported into NZ can push up costs for people and families needing to buy a car. Import passenger registrations have fallen from around 165,000 in 2017 to 85,000 as people increasingly keep their current car for longer, putting off upgrading to newer, safer models.
summary.how: This party would introduce an affordability test for imported cars. This test would flag a regulation if it is seen to reduce supply, thus increasing the prices of used cars.

act.statement: Freeze the minimum wage for three years

summary.why: This party says that higher minimum wages can decrease the demand from businesses for workers to employ. The subsequent unemployment disproportionately burdens young people.
summary.how: This party would freeze the minimum wage at its current rate for three years. This would cause the minimum wage to lose value due to inflation,  allowing more headroom in budgets for employers to bring on more staff, including younger people.

sources.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

act.statement: Introduce a training wage

summary.why: This party says that the minimum wage can increase wage costs at the expense of employing someone new. Young people are less experienced and more likely to struggle to find a job. Younger workers have less experience, need more training and are more costly to hire.
summary.how: This party would establish a training wage at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20, available for their first 12 months with an employer. Standard protections would still apply with the new lower wage rate.

sources.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

act.statement: Protect employers from personal grievances

summary.why: This party says that employers can worry about discussing the end of an employment relationship. The party also says that once a 90-day period has passed, employers should be able to move on without fear of personal grievances being taken up against them for workers they have stopped employing.
summary.how: This party would allow protected employment exit negotiations. It would limit the time to take a personal grievance to the Employment Relations Authority to 90 days after it is raised, while retaining the existing rules for sexual-harassment grievances.

act.statement: Make unions collect their own fees

summary.why: This party says that that the relationship between a union and its members is a private association between them and does not concern the employer.  It is unreasonable to expect union fees to be collected through payroll deductions administered by the employer.
summary.how: This party would ensure that employers were not made by law to facilitate the financial relationship between unions and members. Unions would have the ability to set up their own financial capacity through online banking instead.

act.statement: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and NZ's net zero goal

summary.why: This party says that NZ should play its part to reduce emissions but only in line with what other trading partners do, so that the country is not at a competitive disadvantage. The net zero target is arbitrary, and emissions reductions should be weighted in terms of trade.
summary.how: This party would repeal the current Zero Carbon Act and adopted a trade-weighted approach to emissions reduction instead. The net zero by 2050 goal would be removed, and New Zealand would only do what its trading partners are doing.  This party would also protect NZ workers at risk of losing their jobs in high-emissions industries like steel production, so that these industries face lower carbon prices or none at all and are not at a competitive disadvantage.

act.statement: Remove the carbon price floor and return ETS profits to households

summary.why: This party says that the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) acts as a "carbon tax", with a minimum price for carbon credits set by the government. This means the auctions do not work properly and raises the price of goods and services. The supply of carbon credits should be increased and the profit returned as a refund to New Zealanders.
summary.how: This party would remove the price floor from the Emissions Trading Scheme to place downward pressure on the carbon price. 100 percent of the money from the carbon auction would be returned to New Zealanders as a tax refund. If the amount became so low that the refund was impractical to deliver, it would mean prices had fallen so that people had lower prices for goods and services and would no longer need the tax refund.  Conversions of farmland to permanent forest for creating carbon credits would be discouraged.

act.statement: Introduce noise-detecting cameras

summary.how: This party would introduce noise-detecting cameras in place of present police officers. These cameras would feature microphones, video and number plate recognition. act.statement: Encourage people generating power to sell it to the grid

summary.how: This party would establish an accreditation process for contractors who wish to enter the market for the connection of land/housing to power lines. The party claims that this process will better allow power line companies to offer more choice in contractors for their consumers.

act.statement: Commission Parliament to explore a deal with Meta for young people on social media

summary.why: This party says that proposals to emulate Australia's social-media ban for under-sixteen-year-olds come with privacy concerns. summary.how: This party would ask Parliament to investigate forming a similar settlement with Meta which would include changes seen in the United States. Changes would include a default two-hour daily limit for teenagers, locking most teen accounts between midnight and 6 am, switching off push notifications overnight and during school hours, and giving parents greater power to supervise and restrict their children’s accounts. summary.how: This party would purchase land from the University of Auckland and its Epsom campus and repurpose the facility into a co-ed high school. Parents would retain eligibility for the grammar school's school zone.

act.statement: Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from infrastructure planning law

summary.why: This party says that spiritual beliefs, particularly those that come from Te Ao Māori, should not be used as the basis for assessing an infrastructure project's viability. It says that planning law should regulate effects that can be identified, measured and tested, and protect rights recognised by law. It should not require planners, councils or judges to rule on spiritual or religious beliefs.
summary.how: This party would exclude purely spiritual and religious effects. It would legislate that a religious or spiritual belief, or a claim of spiritual harm, could not on its own be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information, or imposing a consent condition. The rule would apply equally to all religions and belief systems and use the test already applied under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. It would also ban compulsory spiritual observances. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or fund a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. Anyone who wants to do these things voluntarily could still do so.

green.statement: Return the tax rate to 33 percent for New Zealand's biggest corporations

summary.why: This party says that multi-national businesses send profits offshore and don't pay the same taxes as local businesses. This increases prices and decreases wages. Lower corporate taxes have not led to improvements for working New Zealanders. The corporate tax rate increase would only be on the 0.7 percent biggest businesses in NZ, including banks, supermarkets and energy companies. This would level the playing field for small and medium businesses.
summary.how: This party would increase the tax rate to 33% for large corporations while keeping it at 33% for small and medium businesses. A bank levy of 0.06 percent would be added to the liabilities of the four big banks (ANZ, BNZ, Westpac and ASB).

green.statement: Establish a government backed clean energy loan scheme

summary.why: This party says that this policy would help make household power bills more affordable so people would not have to choose between heating or eating. This party says that since 2021, 100,000 more households cannot afford to heat their home and 76,000 could not pay their bills on time. The easiest way to lower household power is to help people generate and store solar power but most people are barred from this due to the expensive upfront cost of equipment purchase.
summary.how: This party would establish a government-backed loan scheme to enable zero-interest clean energy loans for up to 90% of homeowners. Homeowners can use these loans for rooftop solar, batteries and making energy efficiency upgrades. Some borrowers will have the option to defer repayments until property sale, while loans will be paid off over time via a separate levy. Central government would be a 20 percent shareholder, with participating councils and the Local Government Funding Agency (LGFA) splitting the remaining 80 percent. The Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) would implement the scheme.

summary.why: This party says that Māori are two to three times more likely to experience energy hardship compared to the general population. This policy would ensure Māori can access clean energy, resulting in cheaper power bills that also uphold kaitiakitanga, rangatiratanga and tikanga.
summary.how: This party would invest in projects ranging from solar on kaumātua homes and papakāinga (communal housing built by families on ancestral Māori land) to geothermal energy to local distribution solutions that help manage energy on Māori land. This party estimates that this policy would cost $80 million over four years.

green.statement: Establish a publicly-owned Crown entity to invest in renewable generation.

summary.why: This party says that NZ needs a resilient energy system to provide backup renewable power that keeps electricity affordable when hydro lakes are low and wind power decreases. Gas historically fills this gap, but gas is being exhausted more quickly than expected.
summary.how: This party would create Kiwipower, a new publicly owned Crown entity that invests in renewable energy generation. Its main focus would be on renewable firming capacity such as geothermal, batteries, demand response, biomass and pumped hydro, to ensure energy demands can be met at all times. Kiwipower would contract firming capacity and make that capacity available to independent generators, retailers and energy users at affordable and transparent prices. Large power companies would be required to provide a portion of their firming capacity to Kiwipower. The entity would be funded by a tax on the wealthy, at an estimated cost $980m over four years.

green.statement: Create a self-governance trust to restore and sustain marae

summary.why: This party says that marae are a key part of New Zealand's national identity for Māori and non-Māori. They are a central hub during states of emergency, serving and connecting communities. Despite this significance, marae across NZ are ageing with failing infrastructure and need long-term financial support to be sustained.
summary.how: This party would create Te Rangatiratanga Trust, which provides immediate support and long-term funding certainty for marae, owned and operated by hapū and iwi. The Crown would provide $2.44bn to establish the trust and two funds: Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration Fund, which would provide $400m over four years for urgent needs, and Te Tōtara Haemata Intergenerational Fund, to protect and grow capital for future generations. The latter would be funded by returns from a $2bn diversified portfolio. Trust funding decisions would be made independently of ministers and successive governments.

green.statement: Support Māori autonomy in their responses to climate change

summary.why: This party says that climate change is damaging Māori customary practices, cultural identity, well-being and connection to the land. Historical and current injustices have also weakened the resources of Māori communities and businesses to mitigate and adapt to climate change.
summary.how:

It would also fund Māori-led initiatives for transitioning away from fossil fuel and agribusiness ventures into sustainable industries.

green.statement: Include agriculture, shipping and aviation in emissions calculations and reduction efforts

summary.why: This party says that the overarching legislation for addressing climate change is too weak to actually prevent the negative impacts we are seeing and will see more in the future. Large, profit-driven corporations are influencing decision-makers reducing the voice of individuals and communities. NZ's dependence on fossil fuel is also deeply embedded in all parts of our economy, which is a barrier to economic resilience and limits the effectiveness of climate policies.
summary.how:
This party would require the implementation of Te Tiriti o Waitangi and co-governance in decision-making and extend the Climate Change Response Act to cover every sector and all greenhouse gases. 
Domestic air and shipping fuel emissions would also be included in calculating emissions for both the public and private sectors. Non-forestry carbon sequestration technologies would be on a pathway to net carbon-zero, and emission reduction targets would be transparent and align with global obligations. Purchases of offshore emissions credits would be allowed only as a last resort. There would be robust monitoring and enforcement of the legal obligations for emissions reduction contained in the Act.

green.statement: Focus on reducing gross emissions, rather than net emissions

summary.why: This party says that the overarching legislation for addressing climate change is not strong enough to prevent the negative impacts we are seeing and will see more in the future. Economic activity, linked to greenhouse gas emissions, is prioritised over the voices of the community.
summary.how: This party would ensure the Emissions Trading Scheme is sufficient to meet reduction obligations under the Climate Change Response Act and can compensate for climate change mitigation and adaptation costs. green.statement: Ensure all sectors are covered by an effective emissions pricing system

summary.why: This party says that all sectors need to be incentivised to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, in order to prioritise the health of the environment and humanity over profit.
summary.how: This party would phase out the free allocation of NZUs to emission-Intensive and trade-exposed industries, and implement a framework for pricing agricultural greenhouse gas emissions. It would also include emissions from international aviation in pricing schemes. Marine-based 'blue carbon' - carbon dioxide captured and stored by the world's ocean and coastal ecosystems - would be included in the ETS. Alternative emissions pricing mechanisms would be implemented when the ETS is not doing its job in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, existing foresters would received equitable treatment from any changes in forestry-related carbon offsetting systems.

green.statement: Advocate internationally for strong climate action from other countries and partners

New Zealand is relatively wealthy but currently ranks poorly against other countries for its climate change policies. summary.how: This party would advocate internationally for the strengthening of international climate agreements and encourage all countries to increase their Nationally Determined Contributions so that global emissions halve by 2030 and reach net carbon-negative by 2050 to limit global average temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius. green.statement: Prohibit palm kernel expeller (PKE) imports
