green.statement: Amend the definition of consent to be free and voluntary

summary.why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing and women and gender minorities should be safe, respected and valued.
summary.how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to amend the definition of consent and affirm that consent must be free and voluntary, and can be withdrawn at any time.

green.statement: Criminalise coercive control

summary.why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing and women and gender minorities should be safe, respected and valued.
summary.how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to criminalise coercive control.

green.statement: Extend paid parental leave to 15 months

summary.why: This party says that women and families deserve to be safe and supported. Women deserve to get paid for their work, and compensated for time at home carrying out the essential work of caregiving.
summary.how: This party would increase paid parental leave to 15 months for the primary caregiver, and have additional ring-fenced leave for partners. This party would also increase payments.

green.statement: Fill empty stores by changing retail lease rules and addressing vacant buildings

summary.why: This party says that towns and cities need help to keep their centres vibrant. Empty shops are apparent on most main streets because of high rents set when the market was stronger. Many commercial leases don't allow for a rent review below the level set.
summary.how:
This party would ensure market rent reviews can lower rents as well as raise them. This will apply to both new and existing leases for businesses with a turnover of under $30m. 
It would also give councils the power to auction leases on shops that have been empty for more than a year, and a low-cost tribunal will be established for commercial lease disputes.

sources.title: 'Greens announce plan for city centre vibrancy ', 19 September 2026 (accessed 22 September 2026)

green.statement: Refuse to use AI for decisions on welfare payments

summary.why: This party says that the government's push for automated decision erroneously left tens of thousands of financially vulnerable people without funds.  Similar issues overseas have proven why decisions on who receives financial support should not be left to algorithms.
summary.how: This party would not use AI and automated decision making for welfare payment decisions such as cancelling, suspending, or reducing welfare payments, or imposing benefit sanctions.

sources.title: 'Green Party pledge to remove AI from welfare payment decisions', 11 September 2026 (accessed 16 September 2026)

green.statement: Recognise Palestine as a state and sanction Israel

summary.why: This party says that that NZ should be an independent voice against global atrocities, authoritarians, and imperialist ambitions. This party says most United Nations member states have already recognised Palestinian statehood.
summary.how: This party would recognise Palestine as a state and pass a bill drafted by this party to sanction Israel.

sources.title: ' Govt’s empty words do nothing to stop genocide in Gaza ', 11 August 2025 (accessed 23 September 2026)

green.statement: Rewrite foreign policy to oppose imperialism

summary.why: This party says that war and authoritarianism is rising globally, and NZ should be an independent voice for peace, freedom, democracy, and should speak out against nuclear weapons and American militarism. This party says foreign policy should challenge imperialism that creates chaos and hardship, and should always support countries facing conflicts and human rights abuses.
summary.how: This party would withdraw NZ from the Five Eyes security alliance and decline to participate in AUKUS, as part of efforts to step away from military and security frameworks with the United States. This party would rewrite NZ's foreign policy to stand against human rights abuses and focus on upholding peace and justice, and would have the Defence Force focus on climate change, humanitarian responses and environmental monitoring.

green.statement: Support sovereignty and independence in the Asia-Pacific

summary.why: This party says that that NZ should work with Pacific neighbours to create a greener, safer, and more just world. This party says NZ should be a world leader on issues of climate action, protection of nature and indigenous and human rights, and should work to uphold the international rule of law and collective obligations towards issues like climate change.
summary.how: This party would support Pacific sovereignty, independence, and oppose militarisation in the Pacific. This party would also support decolonisation and democracy movements globally, including those of indigenous peoples in Asia-Pacific region and work to urgently progress climate change initiatives through international institutions. It would support calls for West Papua to be independent of Indonesia, and for French-ruled Polynesian islands to be independent and call for an indigenous-led human rights investigation and a visit from the UN's Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous People.

green.statement: Increase democratic scrutiny of trade agreements

summary.why: This party says that that NZ should have an independent approach to foreign affairs and trade that focuses on climate action, nature protection, indigenous and human rights.
summary.how: This party would implement a suite of measures including increased democratic scrutiny of trade agreements, and enforceable recognition of Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations, workers’ rights, human rights and climate commitments in trade agreements.

green.statement: Decriminalise cannabis for personal use

summary.why: This party says that harmful drug use must be treated first as a health issue, rather than a criminal justice issue. While there can be adverse consequences from drug use, not all drug use is abusive or problematic, and evidence indicates making substance use illegal makes it harder for people to seek help. In terms of drugs, cannabis causes far less harm than alcohol, methamphetamine, cocaine, or tobacco.
summary.how:
This party would regulate cannabis for legal personal use, with a legal age limit. Previous criminal convictions for these offences are removed from all records. Cultivation for personal use would generally be no longer illegal, and an evidence-based approach would be taken on which regulatory model best minimises harm. This includes improving drug-driving laws and providing education on the harmful effects of heavy or prolonged cannabis use.
Medicinal cannabis would be accessible and affordable for patients.

green.statement: Increase free public health services

summary.why: This party says that everyone should have reliable access to public healthcare, including during and after civil emergencies. This party says hospitals and GP clinics are stretched and over-capacity, and suffering from under-investment from successive Governments. It says private provider costs in healthcare are preventing people from seeking help early, causing health issues to escalate.
summary.how: This party would work towards free public primary healthcare and dental care, that can be accessed by everyone. They would increase focus on prevention and early screening, early diagnosis and treatment of non-communicable diseases, such as kidney disease, cancers, diabetes, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. This party would fund the creation of mobile clinics for health care, mental health, diagnostic services and dental vans, for rural communities and during and after civil emergencies, including by-Māori, for-Māori community clinics. This party would also increase funding for data and digital infrastructure and capability in the health sector. This party would also regulate providers of private infrastructure and hold them to high standards of privacy.

green.statement: Simplify funding for Hauora Māori providers

summary.why: This party says that Hauora Māori and social service providers of healthcare are underfunded and restricted by contracts that are overly prescriptive. This party says Māori are underserved by the health system, and that progress to provide equitable healthcare has been undone. This party says kaupapa Māori health services should be supported to end health inequalities.
summary.how: This party would stop overly prescriptive Hauora service contracts. This party would simplify and improve funding arrangements for providers of health services for whānau, hapū iwi and hapori. They would commit to working with Iwi Māori partnership boards and Hauora Māori to do this.

green.statement: Improve wages and staffing for health providers

summary.why: This party says that that under-investment in health services has led to an understaffed hospital workforce and GP clinics that can't accept new enrollments. They say there are unsafe conditions for health workers and lengthy wait times. This party says everyone should be able to access timely healthcare from a supported workforce
summary.how: This party would ensure all health workers have fair wages. They would fund pay parity for primary care and hauora providers. This party would set safe staffing levels, to improve worker wellbeing and quality of care.

green.statement: Increase funding for Pharmac

summary.why: This party says that that Pharmac should invest in new health care devices and medicines so that treatment and quality of life for patients improves.
summary.how: This party would increase sustained funding for Pharmac.

green.statement: Expand the conditions that pharmacies can treat

summary.why: This party says that that pharmacists should help treat common health issues and should be encouraged to give appropriate medical advice. This party says they should be compensated fairly to do so.
summary.how: This party would Expand the Minor Health Conditions Service to help pharmacies treat common health issues, and update the Integrated community pharmacy services agreement to compensate pharmacists fairly.

green.statement: Support migrant workers to residency

summary.why: This party says that that people coming to NZ for work should have fair and achievable pathways to residence. The party says that migrant workers are not disposable, yet they face exploitation, are denied basic rights and are unfairly targeted by immigration compliance officers.
summary.how: This party would create new residency pathways for migrants who have settled in NZ long-term, including those whose visas have expired. This party would also allow migrant work visa holders to switch employers and would end the 12-month stand-down period requiring workers to leave the country between visas.

green.statement: Abolish acceptable standards of health requirements for migrants and refugees

summary.why: This party says that says that migrants and refugees with health conditions or disabilities are discriminated against by the acceptable standards of health requirements.
summary.how: This party would abolish the Acceptable Standards of Health requirements for visa applicants.

green.statement: Support families of migrants and refugees to get visas

summary.why: This party says that says that nobody should be unfairly separated from their families or communities. This party says people who flee war or persecution to seek asylum in New Zealand should be supported and treated with dignity.
summary.how: This party would clear the backlog for refugee family reunification, including resourcing Immigration New Zealand to clear the backlog of tier 1 and 2 family reunification categories and process asylum claims quickly. This party would restore birthright citizenship, expand work rights for partners, remove income barriers to supporting a parent visa, and stop detention and electronic monitoring of asylum seekers.

green.statement: Increase the refugee quota

summary.why: This party says that that people who fear for their life in their country, should be supported to seek a better life in NZ. They say people escaping war or persecution should be supported to rebuild their lives as part of our communities.
summary.how: This party would progressively increase the refugee quota to 5,000 by 2029. This party would also increase funding for refugee resettlement programmes and create a new humanitarian visa for family of New Zealanders in conflict zones.

green.statement: Create an immigration system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi

summary.why: This party says migrants and refugees should be supported to rebuild their lives in NZ.
summary.how: This party would implement Māori aspirations for an immigration system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi. It would develop resources and decision-making with iwi and hapū to strengthen traditional whanaungatanga connections. This party would also provide Te Tiriti education to new migrants and refugees.

green.statement: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficaries

summary.why: This party says that everyone has a right to a liveable income that guarantees enough for food, safe housing and good quality of life. This party says the cost of living has got worse, and thousands of children go to bed hungry and families are struggling to pay rent or mortgages.
summary.how: This party would increase benefits to liveable rates and individualise benefit entitlements. This party would also abolish benefit sanctions. The party would reform the Social Security Act to uphold dignity of people seeking support and ensure everyone has a secure income, and implement a high-trust working model at work and income. This party would also overhaul recoverable assistance grants, write off existing debt to MSD and ban attachment orders against beneficiaries.

green.statement: Introduce a tax for net wealth over $10m

summary.why: This party says a wealth tax is part of a fairer tax system, that can reduce income inequality and ensure everyone has enough to live. This party says multi-millionaires pay $9 in tax for every $100 they make, while teachers pay $22 in tax for every $100 they make. This party says a wealth tax makes super-rich New Zealanders pay a fair share.
summary.how: This party would introduce a 2.5 percent tax on net wealth worth over $10m, with an exemption for the family home.

sources.title: 'Greens commit to tax the super-rich and large corporates fairly, cut income tax for 96% ', 21 June 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)

green.statement: Expand ACC to cover income support and treatment

summary.why: This party says that that everyone deserves a livable income if they are unemployed, disabled, sick or a caregiver.
summary.how: This party would extend ACC to cover income support and treatment for injuries, disability and illness, regardless of origin.

green.statement: Strengthen working for families

summary.why: This party says that that families are struggling to pay rent or mortgages, to feed their children, or to warm their homes, as the cost of living has worsened. This party says that families should be looked after at every stage of life.
summary.how: This party would increase the working for families rate, reduce abatements and extend tax credits to families who are unemployed.

green.statement: Prioritise rehabilitation for convicted offenders

summary.why: This party says that rehabilitation is important to keep communities safe. It says current approaches to justice neglect rehabilitation, which causes more harm and hardship for communities.
summary.how: This party would resource evidence-based rehabilitation for anyone convicted of an offence. Tikanga based and restorative justice solutions, like Te Pae Oranga, would be available to anyone to access. This party would also improve community re-integration support for offenders leaving the criminal justice system, and would increase the Steps to Freedom grant to cover at least 30 years of inflation.

green.statement: Increase accountability in policing

summary.why: This party says that the justice system should be safe, equitable and fair. This party aims to meet the basic needs of communities in order to prevent crime happening in the first place.
summary.how: This party would require body cameras for frontline police and strengthen the powers of the Independent Police Conduct Authority. The party would also deliver de-escalation and trauma training for police, and increase resourcing for Māori Wardens and Pacific Wardens.

green.statement: End military-style academies for young offenders

summary.why: This party says that says the justice system should be fair and equitable. This party says people should not be punished for being poor, and communities are safer when young people have access to food, healthcare, education and have a safe home environment.
summary.how: This party would end military-style academies for young people and raise the age of criminal responsibility. This party would also ban young people being detained alongside adults. This party would expand access to specialist youth courts, including the Rangatahi and Pasifika Courts, Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court, and New Beginnings Court, so young people across NZ could access them.

green.statement: Improve accessibility to justice and legal assistance

summary.why: This party says that the justice system should be fair and equitable, and communities should be supported to prevent crime happening in the first place.
summary.how: This party would expand the district court initiative, Te Ao Marama, to all courts in New Zealand. This party would also extend legal aid and duty lawyers, better resource community law centres and make applications for protection and parenting orders free.

green.statement: Reduce restrictions on the decisions judges can make

summary.why: This party says that that laws restricting the decisions a judge can make about sentences have caused more harm and hardship. This party says bias and discrimination in the justice system should be addressed.
summary.how: This party would help enable judicial discretion in sentencing. This includes ending mandatory minimum sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence discounts, three strikes and limits on when home detention can be imposed instead of imprisonment.

green.statement: Extend hate speech laws

summary.why: This party says that that everyone deserves to live free from violence, harm and discrimination.
summary.how: This party would extend hate speech laws to cover religion, gender, disability and rainbow communities. This party would implement this alongside other recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019.

green.statement: Implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019

summary.why: This party says that that everyone deserves to live free from violence, harm and discrimination.
summary.how: This party would implement all recommendations from the royal commission of inquiry, including passing hate speech laws, and continuing to oppose possession of military-style semi-automatic firearms.

green.statement: Implement recommendations of Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care

summary.why: This party says that that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into abuse in care was a harrowing account of how society and the Government failed, and must change. The party says survivors have called for all 138 recommendations to be implemented.
summary.how: This party would implement all recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, in consultation with people with lived experience of abuse in care.

sources.title: 'One year on from apology, Government still missing in action ', 12 November 2025 (accessed 23 September 2026)

green.statement: Ban alcohol advertising and sponsorship

summary.why: This party says that says it is important to take an evidenced, harm-reduction approach to alcohol and drugs.
summary.how: This party would would phase out all alcohol advertising and sponsorship, including at sporting and cultural events, and use funding from the alcohol levy to establish a national harm-reduction campaign.

green.statement: Enable licensing for psychedelic treatment

summary.why: This party says that the 'war on drugs' approach from 50 years ago has increased harm and addictions, and diverts money away from public health services. This party supports an evidence-based approach that prioritises people's health.
summary.how: This party would enable a licensing system for psychedelic treatment, and recognise taonga status of our native psylocibin (magic mushroom) species.

green.statement: Reduce nicotine availability and fund culturally responsive services to quit smoking and vaping

summary.why: This party says that that funding for addiction services should be increased, and NZ should take a harm-reduction approach to alcohol and drugs. This party believes young people should be protected from nicotine by stronger regulations for retailers.
summary.how: This party would phase out nicotine availability and fund culturally responsive vaping and smoking cessation services. This party would also implement stronger regulation and enforcement for nicotine retailers.

green.statement: Restore pay equity and negotiate a settlement for care workers

summary.why: This party says that the previous pay equity law better protected care and support workers who look after disabled people, older people and some of the most vulnerable people in New Zealand every day. However, this law was changed in 2025, and since then, these workers have been undervalued. This party believes a carer's pay should reflect the skill and responsibility their jobs demand.
summary.how: This party would restore the pay equity law to its pre-previous-government form. The party would also fund the settlement for the approximately 65,000 care and support workers whose claim was stopped after those changes were made to the law by passing legislation to settle the claim. The final settlement would be agreed through bargaining with the workers and their unions. This party estimates that this policy would cost $1.1 billion a year.

sources.title: 'Greens commit to pay equity for care workers', 1 October 2026 (accessed 02 October 2026)

green.statement: Make public transport free for children and other specified people and cap fares at $2 for adults

summary.why: This party says that New Zealanders deserve a fast, convenient and affordable transport system. It believes that years of underinvestment in public transport have left our cities harder to get around without a car. However, it says our cities have the potential to be accessible, vibrant and connected for locals and visitors. This will make it easier and more affordable for people to get where they need to go using cleaner modes of transport, also helping to cut greenhouse gas emissions.
summary.how: This party would make bus and train fares free for children, teenagers, students, apprentices, Community Service Card holders, and Total Mobility Users, and cap bus and train fares at $2 for adults.

sources.title: 'Green Party launches the transport plan to combat fossil fuel crisis', 4 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)

green.statement: Create improved public transport services between regions

summary.why: This party says that the fuel crisis is costing ordinary people every time they travel. We need transport alternatives that are more affordable, fast, frequent, and reliable. It says communities are currently designed to prioritise working best for cars, when they should be designed to work best for people.
summary.how: This party would fund up to 150 new regional bus services to supplement existing services, extend the Te Huia train to Tauranga with track and tunnel improvements and pilot an overnight passenger train service between Wellington and Auckland. It would also bring back the Southerner train connection between Christchurch and Dunedin.

sources.title: 'Green Party launches the transport plan to combat fossil fuel crisis', 4 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)
'Fast, frequent, affordable public transport for all of us', undated (accessed 05 October 2026)

green.statement: Improve public transport within cities

summary.why: This party says that New Zealanders spend too much time and money sitting in traffic, filling up the car, and waiting for trains and buses. This party says there needs to be more affordable and accessible alternatives to driving a car.
summary.how: This party would deliver immediate improvements to bus routes along the planned Mass Rapid Transit routes in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch and plan and deliver light rail or bus rapid transit in line with the Infrastructure Commission’s preferred option. The party would also fund Wellington’s critical rail renewal work needed to fix broken-down track assets and infrastructure. It would lastly work with Auckland Transport to fund and deliver level crossing removals to allow for more frequent trains, fewer delays, and better safety outcomes.

sources.title: 'Green Party launches the transport plan to combat fossil fuel crisis', 4 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)
'Fast, frequent, affordable public transport for all of us', undated (accessed 05 October 2026)

green.statement: Fund public transport for the regions

summary.why: This party says that regions are often left behind when it comes to public transport infrastructure upgrades, with the focus on major cities. It says that communities living in smaller towns also deserve the opportunity to access affordable and accessible public transport.
summary.how: This party would fund the planned bus improvements in smaller cities and towns in the Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Taranaki, Horowhenua, and Otago. It would also work to revitalise town and city centres and increase safe walking and biking infrastructure.

sources.title: 'Green Party launches the transport plan to combat fossil fuel crisis', 4 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)
'Fast, frequent, affordable public transport for all of us', undated (accessed 05 October 2026)

green.statement: Protect 30% of the Hauraki Gulf by 2030

summary.why: This party says that everyone loves the Hauraki Gulf and we are supposed to protect and look after the things we love. This party wants to restore the marine ecosystem of the Gulf and ensure it is flourishing for generations to come.
summary.how: This party would commit to the Hauraki Gulf Forum's goal of protecting 30% of the Gulf by 2030, as part of its wider plan to protect at least 30% of New Zealand's oceans by reforming marine protected area legislation. It would also remove the ring-net fishing exemption from the Gulf's high protection areas immediately, through a Bill released in early October. Iwi and hapū would be supported to lead ocean protection in the Gulf. As part of its wider conservation policy, the party would also enable the Gulf’s fisheries to be managed according to the health of the entire ecosystem by reviewing the Quota Management System.

sources.title: 'Greens announce plans to protect the Hauraki Gulf', 6 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)
sources.note: greens.org.nz page not retrievable; same press release mirrored on scoop.co.nz

green.statement: Fund and deliver level crossing removals in Auckland

summary.why: This party says that over the last 10 years, there have been almost 70 crashes and hundreds of near-misses at level crossings across Auckland. Removing them will allow for better safety outcomes, more frequent trains and fewer delays.
summary.how: This party would work with the Auckland Council to identify the best options to fund and deliver level crossing removals.

sources.title: 'Greens Commit To Funding And Delivering Level Crossing Removals', 5 October 2026 (accessed 06 October 2026)

green.statement: Guarantee every 16-to 24-year-old who has been out of work for six months a pathway into education, training, or a new job

summary.why: This party says that youth unemployment is at nearly 15 per cent, roughly three times that of the wider working-age population, which is at an 11-year high. Yet there is so much work to be done in New Zealand. This party says it does not make sense, with nearly 100,000 young people not in employment, training or education. A long period without a job at the start of a working life also lowers a person’s wages for years afterwards.
summary.how: This party would establish the Jobs for Young People pilot programme, based on the successful Jobs for Nature model, to support new jobs in businesses, councils, iwi, non-profits or the public sector. It would also scale up funding of the Mayor's Taskforce for Jobs for all 67 councils, connecting young people with local businesses, community organisations, iwi and hapū. Lastly, it would make sure there is a national workforce strategy plan for young people.

sources.title: 'Greens announce jobs guarantee for young people', 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

green.statement: Ensure AI does not replace human judgement or democratic decision-making

summary.why: This party says that artificial intelligence should support human judgement, not replace it. Decisions that affect people's rights, welfare, health, education, employment, or access to public services must remain subject to meaningful human oversight and appeal.
summary.how: This party would require public registers of AI systems used by government agencies with full transparency around AI use, including where in policy processes it has been used, and where or how it has been used to inform decisions. The party would ensure people are held accountable for AI decisions and that everyone has a right to challenge AI-assisted decisions, and to opt out of being subject to AI-assisted decision- making.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)
'Greens will regulate AI for the public good', 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)
sources.note: greens.org.nz page not retrievable; same press release mirrored on scoop.co.nz

green.statement: Refrain from purchasing or deploying autonomous weapons

summary.why: This party says that Artificial intelligence should support human judgement, not replace it, especially when it concerns warfare and the implications of that for the life and wellbeing of humans.
summary.how: This party would refuse to purchase or deploy autonomous weapons systems and support an international ban on these, in the same way the international community has banned chemical and biological weapons.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)
'Greens will regulate AI for the public good', 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

green.statement: Protect data sovereignty

summary.why: This party says that data is a taonga (treasure). The party believes that New Zealanders, iwi, hapū, communities, and creators should retain meaningful control over how data about them is used. Language in particular is crucial to identity and culture, and must be protected from AI.
summary.how: This party would enforce explicit consent standards for AI training data, where appropriate remuneration must be provided for any Intellectual property used for training AI models. The party would ensure there are fines for any breaches, with the Privacy Commissioner given more power to enforce NZ's privacy laws. Government AI systems would be transparent, and there would be specific regulations requiring co-governance and co-development of Māori data and IP to protect Māori data sovereignty. Lastly, private information provided to the government and classified government will not be sent to third parties for model training.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)
'Greens will regulate AI for the public good', 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)
sources.note: greens.org.nz page not retrievable; same press release mirrored on scoop.co.nz

green.statement: Place limits on AI data centres' use of water and electricity

summary.why: This party says that while AI seems like a virtual technology, it actually consumes large amounts of resources, taking up land, using water to cool servers and requiring electricity to power data centres. This party says that any data centres based in New Zealand would need to follow strict regulations to protect the environment.
summary.how: This party would require AI data centres to report on their environmental impact before being built. New facilities would be required to provide new renewable energy to cover their electricity use and their would be community consultation during the consenting process. To increase transparency, this party would require data centres to report their water use publicly.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

green.statement: Ensure news companies are paid by AI companies for their use of AI

summary.why: This party says that AI carries many risks, and can impact how information is understood. It says that news companies generate information and should be compensated by digital AI companies for how much information journalists generate ends up in AI summaries or responses.
summary.how: This party would update and pass the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, requiring AI companies pay local media outlets for data used in their AI summaries.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

green.statement: Encourage the adoption of multiple types of AI

summary.why: This party says that AI companies can concentrate economic power, leading to bad outcomes for workers and individuals. These risks should be regulated by government.
summary.how: This party would encourage the use of public-interest and open-source AI models wherever possible, and mandate the use of multiple and interchangeable AI models to prevent vendor lock-in. It would encourage the use of NZ-based and NZ-focussed large language models, rather than relying on AI tools from overseas companies.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

green.statement: Protect children and worker's rights in the use of AI

summary.why: This party says that AI can concentrate economic power and impact individuals and communities. Power should not be concentrated, and the use of AI should not be at the expense of children and worker's rights.
summary.how: This party would ensure children are not forced to use AI, especially at school, and broadly make sure that AI use around kids is in line with the UNCRC’s Joint Statement on Artificial Intelligence and the Rights of the Child. It would also require that workers are consulted about AI use in their workplace.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

green.statement: Create an AI office and require transparent AI use

summary.why: This party says that people have a right to know when they are interacting with AI and how it is being used. AI content should always be clearly labelled so that people understand when they are using an AI model.
summary.how: This party would create labelling requirements for artificial intelligence, and audit algorithms for high-risk AI systems, so there is monitoring of AI use in the public sector. It would create an AI office within the department of prime minister and cabinet (DPMC) and aim to eventually establish an AI commission with independent powers to conduct audits assurance and education regarding AI use. This party would also collaborate with international best practice like the EU AI Act and build on NZ's work in the Christchurch Call to cooperate with like-minded countries regarding AI regulation and governance.

sources.title: 'Safe, sovereign AI. An AI Plan for Aotearoa' (PDF), 12 October 2026 (accessed 13 October 2026)

green.statement: Strengthen the Zero Carbon Act by requiring the government Budget process to be consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees, gross emissions reduction targets and international commitments.

summary.why: Climate Action: Emissions Reduction — Bold action and solutions that hold polluters to account

green.summary_source: archive (statement is the verbatim "Our plan" commitment from the Green Party Manifesto 2026)

green.statement: 2026 election manifesto: 'A Green government. For all of us.' (38 policy chapters)

summary.how: The party's 43-page (23 PDF spreads) 2026 election manifesto, launched at its AGM on 26 July 2026. It frames the campaign around three priorities (affordable living, healthy nature and 'real democracy'), funded by taxes on the very wealthy and large corporations alongside an income tax cut for most earners, and sets out a short numbered 'Our plan' list in each of 38 policy chapters (Children to Zero waste). Every 'Our plan' commitment is listed individually below under its topic.

green.statement: Tax policy 'A tax system for all of us': wealth tax, capital acquisitions tax, higher tax on big corporates, bank levy, and income tax cuts for 96% of earners

summary.how: The 12-page tax plan (announced 21 June 2026). Revenue measures: a 2.5% tax on the net assets of the super-rich above $10 million (family homes exempt); a capital acquisitions tax on gifts and inheritances over $1 million (family farms and homes exempt); a 33% company tax rate for the largest 0.7% of companies while small and medium firms stay at 28%; a 0.06% levy on the liabilities of the four big banks; enforcing a 5% withholding tax on big tech profits sent offshore; and reversing the coalition's landlord interest-deductibility and bright-line changes. Income tax: a $10,000 tax-free threshold, new stepped brackets and a 45% rate above $160,000. The party's own Parliamentary-Library-based modelling puts the net gain at about $5.1-5.7 billion a year (2027/28-2030/31).

sources.title: A tax system for all of us — Contributing fairly to society (Tax policy 2026)

green.statement: 'Drink Swim Fish' freshwater and oceans policy

summary.how: A 4-page water policy (announced 6 July 2026) aimed at safe drinking water, swimmable rivers and healthier oceans: science-based national freshwater limits including lower nitrate limits, stronger wastewater-discharge rules, phasing out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, phasing out bottom trawling and other destructive fishing, protecting at least 30% of oceans, and reviewing the fisheries quota system.

sources.title: Drink Swim Fish — Fixing the rules for fresh water and oceans

green.statement: 'Power for all of us' energy policy: Kiwipower, Warmer Kiwi Homes expansion, community energy and zero-interest solar loans

summary.how: The 12-page energy policy (announced 20 July 2026). It proposes 'Kiwipower', a publicly owned company to contract and build electricity firming; an expanded Warmer Kiwi Homes insulation/heating programme; $200m for community-owned energy; a government-backed Clean Energy Loans Scheme (modelled as zero-interest, tied to the property) for rooftop solar and other home energy upgrades; and other electricity-market changes. It includes four-year cost tables and says spending would be funded by the proposed super-rich tax.

sources.title: Power for all of us — Lower bills. Cleaner energy. Public ownership.

green.statement: Establish Kiwipower, a publicly owned electricity firming company

summary.how: A 6-page explainer for the proposed publicly owned firming company 'Kiwipower': it would contract access to existing hydro/thermal firming, invest in new renewable firming and storage (geothermal, biomass, batteries, small pumped hydro, demand response) and sell firming at fair prices to independent retailers and large users. Costed at $412.6m opex and $568m capex over 2027/28-2030/31, to be established by the end of 2027. (Image-only PDF; text transcribed by hand.)

green.statement: Te Waonui a Tāne: an ongoing, protected funding source for marae

sources.title: Te Waonui a Tāne — Thriving Marae for Thriving Communities

green.statement: Youth Jobs Guarantee: a job or training pathway for every 16-24-year-old out of work for six months

summary.how: A 7-page jobs policy (published October 2026) guaranteeing every 16-to-24-year-old who has been out of work for six months a pathway into a locally based job or training, delivered with councils and building on the Mayors Taskforce for Jobs. The document's indicative costings rise from $604m in the first year to $1,631m in the fourth.

sources.title: Youth Jobs Guarantee — A guaranteed job for every young person in Aotearoa

green.statement: 'Safe, sovereign AI': regulate artificial intelligence for the public good

summary.how: An 8-page AI plan (announced 12 October 2026). It proposes rules so that AI does not replace human or democratic decision-making (no fully automated decisions with substantive effects in public services), protects data sovereignty, privacy and creators' work, operates within environmental limits (including controls on data centres), shares benefits rather than concentrating them, and is transparent and accountable.

green.statement: 'Affordable food for all of us': KiwiMart public supermarket chain, stronger grocery regulation and a Fair Food Fund

green.statement: Paid placements for trainee nurses, teachers and social workers; abolish the training wage for apprentices

labour.statement: Remove $5 charge for prescriptions

summary.why: This party says that that last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they had been prescribed because they couldn't afford it. Not receiving treatments mean that health problems are exacerbated, and research shows that people who skip medication are more likely to end up in hospital. Making prescriptions free is an upfront cost for the government which removes pressure on the health system.
summary.how: This party would remove the $5 fee for prescriptions of funded medication. This would apply to anyone who is entitled to free healthcare in New Zealand, instead of just people under age 14 and over age 65 and those with Community Services Cards. This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

labour.costing: This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

sources.title: Affordable Healthcare - NZ Labour's Medicard Plan

labour.statement: Make up to three GP visits a year free

summary.why: This party says that many New Zealanders have to choose between medical care and other essentials like food. Some general practices charge nearly $100 per visit. Under the "Medicard" policy programme, anyone eligible for funded healthcare could go to the GP for free at least three times a year. This would be paid for by a capital gains tax.
summary.how: This party would cover three visits a year to a doctor or nurse at the GP clinic where people are enrolled. Already free services like immunisations would not count towards the three-visit total. The "Medicard" card and app would link visits to people's National Health Index number. The three free visits are for each year and do not accumulate and roll over into the next year. This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

labour.costing: This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

labour.statement: Create a 28% capital gains tax on commercial and residential properties, excluding family homes

summary.why: This party says that NZ is one of the few countries in the world without some form of capital gains tax. Much of New Zealand's wealth is held in property rather than enabling economic growth. A capital gains tax would increase New Zealand's productivity and make housing more affordable. Money raised from the tax would be invested in healthcare.
summary.how: This party would introduce a 28% tax on commercial properties and residential investment properties. Family farms, homes, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, gifts, and personal items would be exempt. The tax would only apply to people who own multiple properties or commercial properties, and only to profits made after 1 June 2027.

sources.title: Release: Targeted tax to grow the economy and fund free doctor’s visits

labour.statement: Introduce a $20 weekly fare cap on public transport

summary.why: This party says that a cap on public transport fares will help address the everyday struggles New Zealanders face as a result of a high cost of living.
summary.how: This party would introduce a weekly fare cap of $20 on public transport in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch. Everywhere else in New Zealand would see a weekly fare cap of $10. This would begin on 1 July 2027. Once the caps are reached, the rest of that week's trips would be free. There would be no sign-up required; transport users would use their public transport card or payment method as usual for public buses and trains and some ferries.

labour.statement: Ensure all referred maternity scans are free

summary.why: This party says that that pregnant people should not have to worry about money to know their baby is healthy, with each scan currently costing an average $90. No mum would have to skip a scan because they can't afford it.
summary.how: This party would make every referred maternity scan by a doctor, midwife or specialist free in NZ. All a pregnant person would need is a Medicard. To grow the relevant workforce and ease the pressure on hospitals, 24 paid trainee sonographer positions would also be funded, costing less than $3 million a year. This policy would be funded by the party's targeted capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $28.6 million a year.

labour.costing: Within the existing $40 million a year rebate budget.

labour.statement: Require a small-business impact check before new laws and rules

summary.how: Under Small Business First, ministers and agencies would have to consider the impact on small businesses before new laws, regulations and procurement rules are approved.

labour.statement: Keep the operating allowance at $2.4b and fund commitments within existing allowances

summary.how: Labour's Fiscal Plan keeps the operating allowance at the $2.4 billion per Budget set at Budget 2026 and fits its announced capital commitments (about $4.1 billion) within $12 billion of future capital allowances; Labour says the plan was independently reviewed by accounting firm Hall Chadwick.

labour.costing: See Fiscal Plan section above.

labour.statement: Reverse planned public service cuts

labour.statement: Support the NZ-India free trade agreement (with conditions)

labour.statement: Lobbying register, code of conduct and stand-down period for ex-ministers

sources.title: Speech: Trust in Government - Chris Hipkins

labour.statement: Limit parliamentary urgency

summary.how: Urgency would be restricted to genuine emergencies, fixing urgent errors, Budgets and a 100-day plan signposted before the election, and rushed laws would be sent back to select committee.

labour.statement: One person, one vote in local elections

labour.statement: Reform the UN Charter and back the WHO

summary.how: Labour would support reviewing and "maturing" the UN Charter, support the World Health Organization and adopt the updated WHO health regulations.

labour.statement: Push for a ban on lethal autonomous weapons and parliamentary scrutiny of military deployments

summary.how: Labour would seek an ICJ advisory opinion on the legality of lethal fully autonomous weapons and support international efforts to ban them, establish clear parliamentary scrutiny if New Zealand joins armed conflicts, and strengthen oversight of payloads launched from New Zealand.

labour.statement: Human rights defenders programme and recognition of gender apartheid

summary.how: Labour would set up a programme (including safe haven) for human rights defenders, strengthen advocacy for democracy and human rights including in Myanmar, and advocate for gender apartheid to be recognised in the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty.

labour.statement: Re-engage in climate diplomacy and back the global transition away from fossil fuels

summary.how: Labour says it would re-engage strongly in international climate diplomacy and support the global transition away from fossil fuels.

labour.statement: Not join AUKUS

summary.how: A Labour Government would not join pillar one (nuclear-powered submarines) or pillar two of the AUKUS security pact.

labour.statement: End annual benefit renewals for people with permanent disabilities

summary.how: Labour would end annual benefit renewals for people with verified permanent disabilities and work towards systemic change so disabled people can move into open employment.

labour.statement: At least 25% of new Kāinga Ora homes to be accessible

summary.how: Labour would require at least a quarter of new Kāinga Ora builds to be accessible.

labour.statement: Strengthen disability rights in law

summary.how: Labour would require agencies to produce Enabling Good Lives impact assessments, targets and actions; amend the Human Rights Act to define reasonable accommodation and treat denying it as discrimination; progress incorporating the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities into law; and build disabled leadership capacity.

labour.statement: $950m Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency

summary.how: From Labour's first Budget in 2027, a $950 million Crown guarantee for CHFA social bonds would let community housing providers borrow more cheaply; Labour cites a CHFA estimate that for every 11 homes built the saving could pay for a twelfth.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Make possession, cultivation and use of cannabis free from prosecution

summary.why: The ALCP says cannabis prohibition is unworkable and discriminatory, wastes public money and fuels the black market.
summary.how: Part of the party's 'Policy Minimum Programme': no prosecution for possessing, growing or using cannabis and cannabis/hemp products.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Create regulated R18 cannabis commerce like alcohol and tobacco, but with no promotion

summary.why: The ALCP says cannabis prohibition is unworkable and discriminatory, wastes public money and fuels the black market.
summary.how: Legal adult-only sales with no advertising or promotional aspects, with details fine-tuned by a policy council.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Provide for medicinal cannabis, including home-grown medicine and prescribed preparations

summary.why: The party says legal access would promote safer modes of use such as vaporisation and mouth sprays.
summary.how: Establish therapeutic applications of cannabis, allowing both home-grown medicinal cannabis and prescribed preparations.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Enable full-scale hemp production, prioritising local low-cost biofuel, fibre and hurd

summary.why: The party says hemp would create jobs (especially in depressed regions), cut emissions and pollution, save forests and improve soils.
summary.how: Allow full-scale cannabis-hemp farming and use, with priority for localised biofuel production and fibre and hurd for building materials, paper, plastics and textiles; hemp seed as food.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Expunge all cannabis convictions and apologise for prohibition

summary.why: The party says up to 20,000 people a year are convicted of cannabis offences and that Māori are four to five times more likely to be convicted.
summary.how: Wipe all cannabis convictions; the 2020 addendum adds that apologies must be made for the injustices of prohibition.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Hold a prohibition 'truth and reconciliation' commission

summary.why: The party says Parliament has a duty to challenge injustice and break down prejudice.
summary.how: A full commission on prohibition 'in the interests of accountability'.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Set up a tobacco, alcohol and cannabis authority (Drugs Policy Council) to regulate recreational substances

summary.why: The party says credible, harm-reduction drug education is impossible under current 'double standards'.
summary.how: A single regulator to develop the regulatory framework for recreational substances, with 'adults only' enforcement and honest drug education in schools funded from prohibition savings.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Redirect prohibition enforcement money to health, education, community and serious crime

summary.why: The party says police would be freed up for 'real crime' and public trust in the law would improve.
summary.how: Shift funds currently spent enforcing cannabis laws into health, education, community and employment, and more police and court resources for serious crime.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Stop overseas cannabis offences being a barrier to immigrating to New Zealand

summary.why: The party says it has no other immigration position beyond inclusiveness and tolerance.
summary.how: Cannabis offences in other jurisdictions should not bar migrants.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Reallocate drug-war resources to border security and civil defence

summary.why: The party says the international war on drugs aids organised crime and terrorism.
summary.how: Resources freed by ending the cannabis 'drug war' would strengthen border security and civil defence.

legalise-cannabis.statement: Allow at least five cannabis plants per household and affordable micro-licences for small growers

summary.why: Part of the party's 2020 'cottage industry' ideas, which it says are still under discussion.
summary.how: A 'bare minimum' five-plant home-grow allowance, affordable micro-licences for existing growers, Kiwi seed strains, safe edibles, quality-controlled retail products and protection against racially loaded enforcement; an age limit more consistent with alcohol and tobacco.

nap.statement: Start a national conversation about governing without political parties ('Exit politics')

summary.why: NAP says parties force voters into 'package deals' and the system is 'better at producing political careers than producing good decisions'.
summary.how: Experiment with citizens' assemblies, deliberative democracy, local decision-making, participatory budgeting, digital consultation and rotating civic representation, with New Zealand as 'a laboratory for innovation in governance'.

sources.title: Not A Party has a radical proposal — leave politics behind (media release, 7 Oct 2026)

nap.statement: Move peacefully to a society based on voluntary cooperation, guided by principles of self-sovereignty and self-government

summary.how: Its listed principles: self-sovereignty, self-government, self-ownership, self-reliance, self-defence, self-control, self-respect, self-help, solidarity and 'safer communities together'.

national.statement: Invest $50m in roads and rail lines to create a transport hub in Rolleston

summary.why: This party says that Rolleston is a well-placed hub for moving goods around, as it is on State Highway 1, the main southern train line, and connected by road and rail to the West Coast. Because many agricultural goods are moved through this area, making it easier to move goods between trains and trucks will increase efficiency and economic opportunity for producers in this area.
summary.how: This party would invest $50m in a road and rail "intermodal hub" in Rolleston. This funding would be dependent on the result of a business case, where private freight companies and customers would also invest in the hub. It would only go ahead with a mix of public and private funding. This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.

national.costing: This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.

national.statement: Widen State Highway 6 in Queenstown and allow the Queenstown Gondola to use public transport funding

summary.why: This party says that Queenstown is growing fast and there is a lot of traffic on the section of road between Hansen Road down to the Five Mile roundabout. This party says this road should be wider, as it carries freight, tourists and workers. The gondola, which reduces traffic as well as being a tourist attraction and the local government should receive funding for it as public transport.
summary.how: This party would commit $25m to increasing the section of State Highway 6 in Queenstown to four lanes. It would also ensure that the Queenstown gondola could access money from the National Land Transport Fund as a public transport service.

national.statement: Improve transport links in the South Island, especially state highway bridges

summary.why: This party says that the South Island is particularly vulnerable to failures in transport networks, particularly given its reliance on several bridges. Earthquakes, flooding, spread-out communities, big rivers and mountains all mean roads and bridges can easily be damaged and communities could face long detours or have no way to get around. Focusing government money on improving the most at-risk parts of the network could make the South Island transport network more resilient.
summary.how: This party would use the next government policy statement on transport to prioritise the South Island road network's most important points, especially state highway bridges.

national.statement: Change the policy settings for farmers leasing high country land from the Crown

summary.why: This party says that the Crown owns 1.2 million hectares of land through the South Island, which is leased to farmers for pastoral grazing. Much of this land is at higher elevations. Farmers need certainty about which kinds of activities they can do on this land without requiring consent. Giving farmers other income sources on this land, like beekeeping or horticulture, would provide farmers with the confidence to invest and diversify.
summary.how: This party would pass a law implementing changed policy settings for the kinds of activity to be carried out on Crown pastoral land, and for when farmers need approval or consent for activities.

These are managed by the Department of Conservation, and while New Zealanders could continue accessing them for free, tourists should pay some costs towards the upkeep. This money would be invested into tourist infrastructure at these locations.

Changing planning rules for town centres would make it easier to convert spaces into new businesses or accommodation. Gravel in riverbeds can be used for aggregate, and removing gravel can reduce flood impacts. In the legislation replacing the RMA, consistent rules for this activity will be applied throughout the country.

Mining projects in the South Island were included in the government's Fast-track approvals law, and a policy statement for mining specifically would emphasise that these projects are important to national exports.

Making sure that data centres are only built when new electricity generation will also be built would give data centres and electricity generators security without making power prices more expensive.

national.statement: Create an ID card for service dogs to access public places

summary.why: This party says that trained and certified service dogs support people with disabilities including blindness and low vision, epilepsy and hearing loss. These animals have the right to access all public places but are sometimes turned away because they are assumed to be pets. An ID card for these animals will ensure that the dogs and their owners can show they have the right to access public places.
summary.how: This party would issue a standardised national card for all owners of certified service dogs. This would make it clear to businesses and other operators that these animals and their owners have the right to be in public places, and would distinguish them from other animals and pets which do not have the same rights.

national.statement: Recognise introduced game species in law

summary.why: This party says that responsibilities for introduced animals are shared between different agencies, which can make management unclear. Species which hunters and anglers appreciate, like trout and deer, are seen only as pests rather than natural resources. Introduced animals should not be seen as pests by default, especially when they are valued for their cultural, economic or caloric potential. It is possible to balance protecting native species and environments and retaining deer to hunt.
summary.how: This party would replace the current "Tahr Control Plan" and seek proposals to recognise further "Herds of Special Interest". Introduced species would be recognised in the law, not just as pests.

summary.how: This party would make the Game Council the statutory manager of introduced game animals in NZ. national.statement: Increase funding for rural doctors and nurses to train in skills for urgent care

summary.why: This party says that people who live in rural NZ should be able to access health care without travelling a long way. Ultrasounds are useful diagnostic tools, and giving rural-based clinicians the ability to use them will make it easier to decide whether they can be treated locally or need hospital care. Currently, 29% of rural clinicians are paying for PRIME emergency response training themselves; government funding for this program could make it easier for rural health professionals to respond to emergencies.
summary.how: This party would invest $2.5m in a ultrasound training programmed called POCUS, aimed at rural doctors and nurses who carry out after-hours care and provide additional funding for rural clinicians to receive PRIME emergency response training. This would train 140 health professionals in ultrasounds and 150 people in emergency response. To increase the workforce in rural health practices, a $6m investment would help rural general practices to get more staff. This party estimates that this policy would cost $8.5m.

national.statement: Increase places for student teachers to train in schools while studying

summary.why: This party says that teachers arrive in schools without classroom experience, impacting learning. The current government has created the Schools Onsite Training Programme so teachers can receive a stipend to spend three days a week in classrooms while training.
summary.how: This party would increase the number of places in the Schools Onsite Training Programme to 704 each year by 2028, focusing on subjects and areas with teacher shortages. It would also add 50 places to the Teacher Bonding Scheme, bringing the total to 235, which is aimed at helping schools with staffing challenges to attract more staff.

national.statement: Increase paid parental leave to 30 weeks by 2029

summary.why: This party says that parents need more flexibility for taking leave, including taking paid leave at the same time as their partner, so they can receive more support if needed. Current arrangements create financial penalties for people who take time off work to care for their children. Both parents should have the opportunity to access parental leave if they choose.
summary.how: This party would increase parental leave to 27 weeks in the 2027 budget, with further increases in 2028 and 2029. This leave could be split between parents or shared in overlapping periods. After returning to work, pay for annual leave would be calculated based on yearly salaries, rather than average pay for parents who have earned less due to taking parental leave. This party would also continue contributing to a parent's Kiwisaver while they take paid parental leave. Eventually, this party would aim to increase paid parental leave to 40 weeks.

national.statement: Specify that an active "yes" is required in laws around sexual consent

summary.why: This party says that NZ law does not define what consent is, but instead says what consent is not. This means that for legal purposes, the absence of a person saying "no" can be considered consent, depending on the circumstance. To create a better system for the victims of sexual offending, and to be in line with other jurisdictions, the definition of consent should be specified in the law.
summary.how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to specify that consent must be actively given, whether through words or actions. Consent is also not permanent; consent given at one point in time, for one action, is not consent for all future actions. The prosecution would still need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that consent wasn't given, and that the defendant didn't believe, on reasonable grounds, that it was.

national.statement: Separate the Foodstuffs business into two nationwide cooperatives

national.statement: Trial digital-first "seamless" travel between NZ and Australia

summary.why: This party says that NZ and Australia are two of the world's most closely connected economies. Citizens of both countries can already use "smart gates" to enter the country without interacting with a border agent. In 2028 NZ and Australia are jointly hosting the Cricket World Cup, which is an opportunity to trial a way to enter the country without needing a paper passport at all.

national.statement: Legislate affordability as a concern of the Electricity Authority

summary.why: This party says that secure energy is important for NZ to grow its economy. More power supply, competition and choice, as well as regulating the right areas, can make power cheaper for New Zealanders.
summary.how: This party would change the law so that "affordability" is a key objective for the Electricity Authority in its role as the sector regulator. Affordability would be balanced with its other objectives of competition, reliability and efficiency.

national.statement: Make the cost of building transmission for new electricity generation consistent for public and private players

summary.why: This party says that affordable and reliable power is essential for growing the economy. However, some of the areas with possibility for new development of wind, solar and geothermal power generation do not have enough transmission capacity. The system of treating transmission as an asset means that one party might pay for building transmission that benefits multiple power companies and developers.
summary.how: This party would amend the Electricity Act and revise the Industry Participation Code so transmission pricing methodology can recover the costs of investments made by parties other than Transpower. Privately funded interconnection investments would be required to use the same pricing method as well. To encourage private investment, there would be a regulatory framework for connecting private transmission to the main grid operated by Transpower.

sources.title: Affordable power Kiwis can rely on

national.statement: Create a single accreditation scheme for power to new developments or houses

summary.why: This party says that connecting a new new home, subdivision, farm, factory or business to the electricity network is often slow and expensive. Customers have little choice in the work, as it is set and priced by the network authority. This area of the electricity industry should be more competitive.
summary.how: This party would establish a single accreditation scheme for connection contractors, which would be independently assessed. Accredited contractors would be allowed to work on any network in the country. People seeking a connection could get quotes for the work from multiple people. Networks would still be allowed to inspect finished work and approve designs, but would be given set timelines for doing so.

sources.title: Affordable power Kiwis can rely on

national.statement: Create a back-up power contract for dry years

summary.why: This party says that NZ uses largely renewable electricity, which is cheap and abundant. However, this power, especially hydro power, can be unreliable when there is a dry spell and the hydro lakes are low. Back-up has historically been provided by gas, but gas stocks are decreasing. As well as a contract for daily peaks, the 4 big power generators should have a contract for covering gaps over the weeks or months of a dry period.
summary.how: This party would require the Electricity Authority to publish a report about the "back-up gap" with the size and timing of generation that is not covered. Along with published data on contract values, lengths and price ranges, this would help electricity buyers, sellers and investors know what is happening. It would require the creation of a back-up contract so that back-up power can be bought by anyone from any retailer on standardised terms. There would be regular auctions for this contract.

national.statement: Review the system that sets electricity lines charges

summary.why: This party says that network charges are responsible for 2/3 of the price increases in power over the past year. This is partially because lines companies charges are set by an independent regulator and the current cap was set in November 2024 when inflation was high. It was designed for a system before solar power, as houses and businesses can now generate as well as consume power.
summary.how: This party would review part 4 of the Commerce Act regarding electricity distribution to see whether the current system is delivering enough value for money for consumers. It would require distribution businesses to approve residential and small business solar connection applications within two working days, with penalties for lateness.

sources.title: Affordable power Kiwis can rely on

national.statement: Allow people with solar generation to sell power to any buyer

summary.why: This party says that the current rules in the electricity sector assumes that power comes from big generators. However, as more people put solar panels on their homes or businesses, the power sometimes flows the other way. Currently, those with solar panels are locked into selling any excess power to the grid to the same company they have an electricity contract with. If these rules were more flexible, people could get a better price for power they generate.
summary.how: This party would give every household and. business the right to sell power to whichever retailer they choose. This would be achieved through a Government Policy Statement, and specific legislation if needed. Lines companies would be required to base any power export limits on the true capacity of their network, and not restrict exports beyond any genuine network constraint.

summary.why: This party says that Jobseeker benefits are not meant as long-term support. The current "invest to save" programme should be continued and extended, with work support targeted to people who have been receiving a benefit for a longer period of time. More intense case management and employment programmes should be used to target the problems preventing people from being employed, and younger people should particularly receive more help. summary.how: This party would target extra case management and employment programmes to people receiving Jobseeker benefits for over 12 months, who are deemed "job-ready". national.statement: Reduce benefit payments for people receiving support for more than 2 years

summary.why: This party says that welfare support should always be temporary, and after a long time receiving a benefit it is hard for people to find work. While the welfare system should provide a safety net, it should not prevent people from seeking work. Decreasing payments for people who have been receiving benefits for more than two years will incentivise these people to seek work. Parents with dependent children would have their payments decreased less than those without children.
summary.how: This party would reduce payments for people who have been receiving Jobseeker benefits for 2 of the last 3 years, even if these periods of support were not consecutive. From April 2028, this party would reduce the rate for single people to the rate for 20-24 year olds; reduce the rate for couples without children, and reduce the Jobseeker rate for parents with dependent children half as much as for those without. The exact reductions would be based on benefit rates in 2028, as the rate changes with inflation. The Supported Living payment would not change. This party estimates this would save $572m over 4 years.

national.statement: Introduce drug testing for people receiving benefits

summary.why: This party says that the intention of Jobseeker benefits is to help people find work, not to provide long-term support. Many types of work require drug tests for workers, so people receiving Jobseeker benefits should also be tested for drugs, to show that they are ready to work. If drug use is a barrier to employment, it should be addressed.
summary.how: This party would institute random drug tests for people on Jobseeker benefits, as part of MSD's broader employment programme. If drugs are detected, a person will be tested again; if drugs are detected again, MSD will conduct a mandatory assessment to see whether drug use is a barrier to employment and whether it should be addressed. If drug use if not addressed, it could result in benefit sanctions, so that payments are reduced or stopped. It is expected that this policy would cost $1.5m per year.

summary.why: This party says that benefits are intended as temporary support until someone is employed again. If someone chooses to leave a job, the current stand-down period of 13 weeks means they cannot receive a benefit for job hunting until this time has passed. In line with the UK's benefit sanctions system, people who repeatedly leave jobs should have a longer stand-down period.
summary.how: This party would increase the current non-entitlement period for people who leave a job from 13 weeks to 26 weeks. Someone who has left a job more than once would not receive a benefit until this time, about 6 months, had passed.

summary.how: Target removal of another $1 billion of non-tariff barriers by 2030, prioritising barriers identified with exporters, with a focus on paperless trade and digital customs, including through the FIT Partnership.

sources.title: National’s 47-point plan to support Small Businesses
Building the Future - New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

national.statement: Negotiate essential-supplies agreements with like-minded partners

summary.why: National says such agreements protect access to critical goods (food, medicines, critical inputs) during global disruption.
summary.how: Use the NZ–Singapore Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies (AOTES) as a template for agreements with other partners and extend the model across the FIT Partnership with shared early-warning systems.

sources.title: Building the Future - New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers
National’s 47-point plan to support Small Businesses

national.statement: Grow services exports to 35 per cent of exports by 2030 and modernise existing free trade agreements

summary.why: National says services exports have grown from about 23% to 27% of total exports and that existing agreements can deliver more value.
summary.how: Drive services exports towards 35% of total export value by 2030; modernise existing FTAs starting with China (a “negative list” approach to services); grow the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement; pursue a CPTPP–EU digital trade agreement; expand CPTPP and RCEP membership.

sources.title: Building the Future - New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

national.statement: Give NZTE a sharper “lead and follow” mandate and run at least 23 trade missions next term

summary.why: National says NZTE should actively lead companies to new markets rather than only follow them.
summary.how: NZTE would proactively identify exporters who could benefit from new FTAs and build sector opportunity maps; NZTE, Investment New Zealand and Education New Zealand would work under one coordinated strategy; at least 23 trade missions would be completed with a sector focus.

sources.title: Building the Future - New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

national.statement: Invest $16 million from the International Visitor Levy to control wild deer, feral goats and other pests

summary.why: National says damaging wild animal populations harm productive land and conservation gains.
summary.how: $16 million over four years from the IVL for coordinated control across public, Māori and private land, starting in the Central North Island and Southern Westland, and finalising a National Introduced Wild Animal Management Framework.

national.costing: $16 million over four years from the International Visitor Levy.

national.statement: Update agricultural vehicle weight rules so modern tractors and harvesters do not need routine overweight permits

summary.why: National says modern farm machinery routinely needs overweight permits.
summary.how: Update the rules while protecting vulnerable roads and bridges; in the meantime NZTA would be directed to improve the permit system.

nz-first.statement: Divide the "generation" and "retail" aspects of power companies

summary.why: This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for power, because four large companies generate 90 percent of NZ's power, controlling the supply and selling the power directly to customers. The party says that this situation results in high prices for households and industry, leading to companies closing down and job losses.
summary.how: This party would replace the current system so that generation and retail are not done by the same companies. This would make sure that the most expensive generator would not set the price for the rest of the market.

nz-first.statement: Guarantee fixed-price contracts for new electricity generation projects

summary.why: This party says that prices for electricity are too high in NZ. Because of the structure of the market with four major companies, it is hard for competitors to enter the market. The "gentailer" companies can hold back supply, making electricity more expensive, instead of investing in more power generation.
summary.how: This party would guarantee long-term, fixed-price contractions for building new electricity generation. The companies building this infrastructure would receive guarantees that their power would be the first to be used when needed. This would make it easier for investors to fund electricity generation projects, and increase New Zealand's energy security and resilience.
